claims.text: Dynamic formation and reduction of surface oxide species modulates adsorption of ethanol-oxidation intermediates on PGM nanoscale catalysts.
Dynamic surface oxides modulate electron- and proton-transfer pathways during ethanol oxidation.
Dynamic surface oxidation governs catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
The initial high-performance PGM nanoscale catalyst has minimal surface oxide under standard fuel-cell electrolyte conditions.
Changing the applied potential window can control formation and reduction of surface oxide layers.
The relevant transient surface oxide can include Pt oxide.
Operating-potential adjustment induces reversible oxidation of the catalyst surface.
A moderate increase in oxide coverage optimizes the binding of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
A moderate increase in oxide coverage optimizes electron- and proton-transfer processes.
Ethanol complete oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
Moderate oxide coverage enhances product selectivity and catalyst durability.
Excessive oxide formation blocks or hinders active sites.
Excessive oxide formation decreases catalytic activity by altering reaction kinetics.
A slightly broadened potential window that promotes controlled oxide formation will increase complete-oxidation selectivity and sustain activity.
Very broad, strongly oxidizing potential windows will degrade performance and durability.
The narrow potential-window baseline limits surface oxidation and corresponds to the catalyst's reported high performance.
The proposed mechanism applies under fuel-cell-like conditions.
The dynamic surface-oxide mechanism may cease to govern behavior at very high potentials, in nonaqueous electrolytes, or in severely oxidizing environments.
The exact optimal potential window and quantitative relationship between oxide coverage and transfer rates are unknown.
A lack of performance change despite substantial measured changes in oxide coverage would falsify the proposed governing role of dynamic surface oxides.
